short: The Sasanian king Shapur I inflicted Rome's worst eastern humiliation, capturing an emperor alive.
full:
The new Sasanian dynasty proved a far more aggressive eastern neighbour than Parthia had been. Shapur I invaded Roman Syria and Mesopotamia repeatedly from the 240s, defeating and killing the emperor Gordian III's forces in 244 and sacking Antioch, one of the empire's largest cities, around 252 and again later in the decade, exploiting the political chaos of Rome's third-century crisis.

The wars culminated in 260 near Edessa, where Shapur destroyed a Roman army and captured the emperor Valerian in person, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner by a foreign power; he died in Persian captivity. Shapur commemorated the victory, alongside triumphs over two other Roman emperors, in a monumental rock relief at Naqsh-e Rustam. The disaster exposed Rome's eastern frontier as dangerously undefended and forced a defence largely improvised by regional powers rather than the imperial centre.
